title: Correlated disorder versus correlated noise: Ordering in active systems
abstract: Can quenched disorder generate ordering in driven systems? Using a recently proposed hydrodynamic model, we show that sufficiently long-ranged quenched disorder can induce long-range order in two-dimensional (2D) nonreciprocal XY systems, even when the clean system exhibits only short-range order at finite noise. Active surfaces tangentially advected by quenched velocities, governed by the same hydrodynamic equation, become statistically flat with super- or subdiffusive relaxation. In three dimensions (3D), quenched disorder combined with nonreciprocity produces a novel transition between strong-coupling and asymptotically noninteracting regimes, supporting either long- or short-range order. In both 2D and 3D, the exponents are nonuniversal, which vary continuously with the degree of transversality of the quenched disorder. The degree of transversality of the quenched disorder can be tuned to induce transitions in the model for fixed disorder and noise variances.
summary: This theoretical work explores how correlated disorder influences ordering in non-equilibrium active systems, specifically using the nonreciprocal XY model. By applying renormalization group techniques, the authors demonstrate that long-range disorder can stabilize long-range order in 2D and 3D, even when the clean system would otherwise exhibit only short-range order. This provides a quantitative framework for understanding disorder-induced order in driven matter.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether quenched disorder can induce long-range order in driven, non-equilibrium systems, contrasting this effect with the influence of long-range noise.
main_result: Sufficiently long-range quenched disorder can induce long-range order in 2D nonreciprocal XY systems, and in 3D, disorder combined with nonreciprocity creates a novel transition between strong-coupling and noninteracting regimes.
method: The analysis employs a hydrodynamic model and utilizes perturbative Dynamic Renormalization Group (RG) techniques to study the scaling behavior of the system parameters.
model_or_system: The primary model is the nonreciprocal XY (NRB XY) system, described by a hydrodynamic equation. The system is driven by quenched disorder (correlated velocities) and potentially long-range noise.
key_observables: Long-range order (LRO) vs. Short-range order (SRO), dynamic relaxation exponents (super/sub-diffusive), and scaling exponents (z, $\chi$).
important_parameters: The disorder correlation exponent ($y$), the noise correlation exponent ($ ar{y}$), and the disorder strength parameter ($\mu$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on a hydrodynamic description and uses perturbative RG methods, assuming non-local correlation functions for disorder and noise.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate phase diagrams in 2D and 3D space (e.g., $y- ar{y}$ or $y-\mu$ planes), mapping out boundaries between LRO and SRO phases based on disorder and noise parameters.
paper_structure: The paper proceeds by analyzing the 2D case to show LRO induction, then extends the analysis to 3D using RG flow equations to map out phase transitions between different coupling regimes.
why_interesting: The study of non-equilibrium phase transitions driven by disorder is crucial for understanding complex active matter systems, which often lack simple thermal equilibrium descriptions.

Phases with positional LRO (blue) and or- intational LRO but positional SRO (green) are marked. The phase boundary is given by χ = 0. The dynamics is super- diffusive everywhere. For the 2D NRB XY model, the phases are phase LRO (blue) and phase SRO (green). (b) For y −¯y plane for a fixed µ with µ < 1. Phases with positional LRO and super-diffusive dynamics (blue), orientational LRO but positional SRO with super-diffusive dynamics (green), orien- tational LRO but positional SRO with sub-diffusive dynamics (red) and orientational SRO (checkerboard)...

FIG. 2: Variation of z with y in 2D for a fixed µ. (a) µ > 1: z monotonically decreases with y, starting from 2 at y →0. (b) µ < 1: z first rises from 2 at y →0, then decreases monotonically with y, crossing 2 at y = 1 −µ to become less than 2. Thus z has a non-monotonic dependence on y. See text.
